query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism expected to operate across the test regime, predicts performance relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, specifies relevant temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing approximately 5 wt% aluminum into the CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy will promote the in situ formation of a continuous, protective Al2O3-rich oxide (glaze) layer during sliding that reduces direct metal-to-metal contact and limits adhesive and oxidative wear, thereby maintaining a lower coefficient of friction and wear rate across the full temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy matrix without additional Al doping.
generation.intervention: Doping the alloy with approximately 5 wt% aluminum.
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests conducted from room temperature up to 800 °C under controlled sliding loads and speeds similar to standard tribological test conditions in ambient or moderately oxidizing environments.
generation.structural_mediator: A continuous, Al2O3-rich oxide layer (glaze) that forms on the worn surface.
generation.mechanism: The higher oxidizability of aluminum accelerates formation of a dense and adherent Al2O3 layer during frictional sliding. This protective layer minimizes direct metal contact and mitigates both adhesive and oxidative wear mechanisms, thereby reducing the coefficient of friction and wear rate. The mechanism leverages the inherent tribo-oxidative processes to ensure coating integrity across a wide temperature range.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the undoped CoCrFeNi alloy, the Al-doped variant is expected to exhibit a significantly lower coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the temperature range, particularly at high temperatures where wear mechanisms become more aggressive.
generation.baseline: Wear performance (COF and wear rate) of undoped CoCrFeNi under similar sliding conditions and across the specified temperature range.
generation.boundary: Experimental evaluation under sliding conditions spanning from room temperature to 800 °C, with applied loads and sliding speeds that mimic typical tribological testing scenarios, and in an environment where oxidation can occur.
generation.uncertainty: There is some uncertainty regarding the uniformity and stability of the Al2O3 glaze layer, particularly at lower sliding speeds or under varying atmospheres, which might affect the consistency of the wear resistance improvement.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one of the base CoCrFeNi alloy and one doped with 5 wt% aluminum. Perform sliding wear tests over a range of temperatures (room temperature to 800 °C) under identical load and sliding speed conditions. Use surface characterization techniques (e.g., SEM, EDS, XRD) to evaluate the oxide layer formation and integrity post wear.
measurements: Wear rate via weight loss or track cross-sectional analysis
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-doped alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in both COF and wear rate, or fails to develop a consistent and protective Al2O3-rich glaze layer compared to the base alloy across the entire temperature range, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

Figure 10b1, b2 illustrates the worn surface shape of the alloys AlCrFeNiCu and AlCrFeNiCo under minimum wear rate conditions. The wear mechanism in these HEAs depends on the worn surface oxide layers. The frictional heat during sliding raises the temperature at the interface, which may encourage the oxidation of the alloying components. The presence of elements such as Cr and Al aids in the development of protective oxide layers. By preventing direct metal contact and lowering the wear rate, these oxide layers may serve as a barrier. However, high loads and speeds have the potential to wear away the oxide layers, exposing the underlying material to more abrasion. Hard asperities or particles that are less deeply buried in the surface are typically abrasive, creating shallow grooves on worn surfaces,. Additionally, microcracks and fissures on the worn surfaces, point to the fatigue wear process. These cracks start because of cyclic loading and recurrent stress concentrations at specific surface locations.
